text: Praise the LORD! Blessed is the one who fears the LORD, who delights greatly in his commandments.
His descendants will be mighty in the land; the generation of the upright will be blessed.
Wealth and riches are in his house, and his righteousness endures forever.
Light dawns in the darkness for the upright, for the one who is gracious, merciful, and righteous.
It goes well with the one who is generous and lends freely, who conducts his affairs with justice.
He will never be shaken; the righteous will be remembered forever.
He has no fear of bad news; his heart is steady, trusting in the LORD.
His heart is secure; he will not fear, until at last he looks in triumph on his foes.

versions.text: His heart is firm; he is not afraid, and in the end he will look in triumph on his foes.
versions.explanation: The Hebrew עַד אֲשֶׁר ("until") expresses that his fearlessness lasts until he sees the outcome; "and in the end" loses the temporal clause. Also, verse 7 already uses "steady" for נָכוֹן, so "secure" better distinguishes סָמוּךְ, and this reads more smoothly aloud.

text: He scatters gifts freely, giving to the needy; his righteousness endures forever, and his horn is lifted high in honor.

versions.text: He gives freely to the poor; his righteousness endures forever, and his horn is lifted high in honor.
versions.explanation: The Hebrew has two verbs, פִּזַּר ("he has scattered/dispersed") and נָתַן ("he has given"), and אֶבְיוֹנִים specifically means "the needy/destitute." The current rendering collapses both verbs into one and weakens the vivid image of open-handed scattering.

text: The wicked sees it and is angered; he grinds his teeth and melts away. The desire of the wicked will perish.

versions.text: The wicked sees it and is furious; he grinds his teeth and wastes away. What the wicked long for comes to nothing.
versions.explanation: תֹּאבֵד means "will perish," a stronger judgment than "comes to nothing"; also וְנָמָס is literally "melts away," which mirrors the imagery of the wicked dissolving before the righteous. "Angered" avoids the somewhat colloquial "furious."
